analysis.one_liner: Lets workers refuse forced arbitration of job disputes and take their case to court.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal arbitration law so that an employer could not force a worker to give up the right to go to court over a job dispute. Arbitration would only happen if, after a dispute arose, both the employer and employee agreed to it in writing — and signing an arbitration clause could never be a condition of employment. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Private-sector workers would gain the right to take an employment dispute to court instead of being locked into arbitration by a contract signed as a condition of getting the job. Under the bill, arbitration could only be used if, after a dispute actually arose, one side asked for it in writing and the other side agreed in writing within 60 days — and no employer could require arbitration as a condition of employment [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would have let an employee say no to arbitration after a dispute arose, unless both sides agreed in writing within 60 days, restoring access to the courts for discrimination, wage, and wrongful-firing claims [S2] [S3].
It would have banned employers from making arbitration a condition of employment, so signing away your day in court could no longer be the price of getting or keeping a job [S2] [S3].
It applied to contracts entered into or renewed after enactment, so it would cover new hires and anyone whose contract was amended, not just people already locked in [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay: they could no longer force every hire to sign away the right to sue, and discrimination, wage, and firing disputes would go to court or jury instead of a private arbitrator chosen under company-drafted contracts. Some of that cost would come back to workers in the form of stronger bargaining leverage.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for both sides; the bill would have required a fresh written agreement after every dispute, adding friction and possibly pushing some unresolved disputes into lengthy litigation [S2].
The bill applied only to contracts entered into or amended after enactment, leaving existing mandatory arbitration clauses untouched [S3].
It died without a single cosponsor and never received a hearing, so its design was never tested or refined through the committee process [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is substantial: forced arbitration clauses cover a large share of the private workforce, and this bill targeted the core of that practice by making arbitration something both sides must agree to after a dispute arises [S2] [S3]. The costs are real but modest — arbitration does have advantages in speed and cost, and the after-the-fact consent requirement could complicate resolving ordinary disputes — and the bill's narrow effective date would have left existing contracts in place. The main problem is not the design but the outcome: the bill never got a hearing, so the tradeoffs were never seriously examined by Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, where it sat until that Congress ended, so it never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrews introduced the bill on February 8, 1999, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1] [S5].
The Judiciary Committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law on February 25, 1999, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors in the House [S4].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still in subcommittee, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or any vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that write mandatory arbitration clauses into employment contracts, which kept their existing system of routing disputes into private, company-controlled arbitration. Workers gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it alone; no other member cosigned it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never reported the bill out for a floor vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
against.role: Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its subcommittee referral; no hearings, markup, or vote followed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and never received a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: U.S. employers using mandatory arbitration clauses
industries.note: The bill would have stripped employers of their ability to require workers to sign away their right to sue as a condition of a job, forcing discrimination, wage, and firing disputes into open court. Employers had a direct financial and legal interest in keeping mandatory arbitration, and the bill's death preserved that system.

Private arbitration firms handle the dispute-resolution business that mandatory employment arbitration clauses generate. Making arbitration voluntary could reduce that guaranteed stream of cases, though employers and employees could still agree to arbitrate after a dispute arises.
